title: Sunda, Upasunda and the hymn of concord
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hookLine: two unbeatable brothers fall out, and the Rig Veda ends praying for concord
carry: pray for concord: one aim, many voices
tomorrow: a schoolboy says God is in everyone. why does that get him in trouble?

lines: ONLY EACH OTHER CAN KILL THEM.
cards: In the Mahabharata, the sage Narada visits the five Pandava brothers with a warning story. Two demon brothers, Sunda and Upasunda, did everything together: ate together, fought together, ruled together.
Their discipline was so fierce that Brahma, the creator, gave them a boon: nothing in the worlds could kill them, except each other. So they conquered the worlds.

So Brahma had the gods' craftsman make a woman of perfect beauty, Tilottama, and sent her walking past them. Both brothers wanted her. They argued, then fought, and the two that no one else could beat killed each other.
Narada tells it because the five brothers share one wife, Draupadi, and he wants nothing ever to split them. The five make a rule to keep the peace among them.

teach.b: Hindu scripture also holds up the opposite of those brothers. The very last hymn of the Rig Veda is a hymn of concord: sam gacchadhvam, sam vadadhvam, sam vo manamsi janatam.

Word by word: go together, speak together, may your minds agree. Two verses on, it asks that people's aims be shared and their hearts alike, so that they may live well together. Notice what it doesn't ask.
Nobody becomes the same person; the verbs stay plural the whole way, many people moving and speaking. It asks for agreement on the way forward.
That's the teaching: in Hinduism, concord, minds meeting on a shared aim, is something you pray for, out loud and together, because the tradition knows exactly how it breaks.
The brothers were of one mind until each wanted the same prize for himself. The hymn asks a group to want one thing for all of them. Here's where it meets now.
Priya's assembly team is fighting. One senior wants to cut half the readings to save time, Sam is furious, and Priya is in the middle. Sunda and Upasunda would fight it to the end.
The hymn says: find the aim you share, a good assembly, and let both voices speak toward it.

how: Some Hindu gatherings and organizations close with verses from this Rig Veda hymn, sam gacchadhvam, sam vadadhvam, said together by everyone present.

games.q: your two cousins are planning a family reunion and can't agree on anything. what would sam gacchadhvam suggest first?
o: find the one aim they share, then let both voices speak toward it.
pick whoever is older and let the other one follow.
cancel the reunion; agreement can't be forced.
games.why: go together, speak together: the hymn prays for a shared aim carried by many voices. Sunda and Upasunda show what happens when each wants the prize for himself.

practice: Pick one conversation in your life that's stuck. If it's part of your practice, say sam gacchadhvam, sam vadadhvam slowly, with the other person in mind. If not, hold its English: go together, speak together.
Then name, silently, the one aim you both share, and one sentence you could say first that moves toward it. Sit with that sentence for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: sam gacchadhvam, go together, from the Rig Veda's closing hymn of concord.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sam gacchadhvam, go together, all of you.

carryVoice: For the road: pray for concord, one aim, many voices. The brothers show how it breaks. Goodnight, or good morning.
